meta.title: Who really said "Be water, my friend"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Bruce Lee really said it — on camera, 9 December 1971. The line was first heard as Longstreet dialogue credited to Stirling Silliphant.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Be water, my friend'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, Bruce Lee said it — on the 9 Dec 1971 edition of The Pierre Berton Show, filmed in Hong Kong. First heard as Longstreet dialogue credited to Stirling Silliphant.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1940–1973 · Hong Kong-American martial artist, actor & filmmaker
answer.sourceLine: Lee says these exact words on camera on the 9 December 1971 edition of The Pierre Berton Show, filmed in Hong Kong — his only English-language television interview. He is reciting, at Berton’s prompting, dialogue he had already delivered as the character Li Tsung in the Longstreet episode “The Way of the Intercepting Fist” (ABC, 16 September 1971), an episode credited to screenwriter Stirling Silliphant.
answer.confidenceText: Verified — Lee demonstrably spoke this wording in a dated, surviving recording. Who first wrote it down is the genuinely open question.

source.excerpt: Empty your mind, be formless, shapeless, like water. Now you put water into a cup, it becomes the cup. You put water into a bottle, it becomes the bottle. You put it in a teapot, it becomes the teapot. Now water can flow, or it can crash. Be water, my friend.
trail: 16 September 1971 — ABC broadcasts Longstreet: “The Way of the Intercepting Fist,” written by Stirling Silliphant, with Bruce Lee as the martial-arts teacher Li Tsung. Wikipedia’s episode listing ↗ This is where the water passage is first heard: a review of the episode quotes Li Tsung’s monologue in full, closing on “Be water, my friend.” Classic Film & TV Café’s episode review ↗
9 December 1971 — the edition of The Pierre Berton Show filmed in Hong Kong, and what remains Lee’s only English-speaking television interview. Wikipedia: Bruce Lee: The Lost Interview ↗
In that interview Berton asks Lee to recall “the lines Stirling Silliphant wrote for you”; Lee answers with the water passage and closes it “Be water, my friend.” Transcript of the exchange ↗

Wikipedia dates the recording’s rediscovery and airing to 2 November 1994, under the title Bruce Lee: The Lost Interview. Wikipedia: Bruce Lee: The Lost Interview ↗ That is the form in which the clip reached the internet. The recording at the Internet Archive ↗
source.excerptNote: Lee did not volunteer this. Berton had just asked him, “Can you remember the lines Stirling Silliphant wrote for you? The key lines” — and Lee prefaced the passage by explaining he was talking to Longstreet, played by James Franciscus. The version heard in the Longstreet episode itself is shorter and differently worded — it drops the bottle clause altogether, and its water can “flow, or creep or drip or crash.” The episode monologue, quoted in full ↗

author.bio: Born in San Francisco in 1940 and raised in Hong Kong, Bruce Lee was a martial artist, actor and filmmaker who died in 1973 at thirty-two. He built Jeet Kune Do — “the way of the intercepting fist” — around the idea that a fixed style is a cage, a conviction Wikipedia summarises as his principle of “the style of no style.” In 1971 he appeared in four episodes of the American series Longstreet; the first of them, “The Way of the Intercepting Fist,” was credited to his own student, the Oscar-winning screenwriter Stirling Silliphant — the collaboration that put the water metaphor on television. The episode table ↗

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Bruce Lee is sound — he says the words on camera, on a dated and surviving tape. What travels alongside the quote is usually wrong in two smaller, more interesting ways.

items.why: The passage was first heard not as a Bruce Lee statement but as dialogue for his character Li Tsung, in an episode credited to screenwriter Stirling Silliphant. Lee appeared in four Longstreet episodes, and Wikipedia’s episode table credits only this one — “The Way of the Intercepting Fist,” the one carrying the water passage — to Silliphant; the other three went to other writers. The episode table ↗ A South China Morning Post feature is built entirely on this point, headlined around how the ‘be water’ quote “from fictional US TV series came to be attributed to him.” SCMP ↗

Sources disagree about how much of the passage Lee put down. Wikiquote’s note says he “was reciting lines he wrote for his short lived role on the TV series Longstreet”; Classic Film & TV Café’s review of the episode says instead that Lee “worked on the script with Silliphant.” On camera, Berton framed them as Silliphant’s lines and Lee did not correct him. Wikiquote ↗ The episode review ↗

What Lee says in the interview is “Be water, my friend” — but the softened “Be like water, my friend” circulates just as widely, including as the standing epigraph on a long-running fan page devoted to this very interview. The two are frequently swapped mid-sentence. An example of the variant ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Lee really did say it, on 9 December 1971 — but he said it as a recitation, prompted by Berton asking him to recall “the lines Stirling Silliphant wrote for you.” Transcript of the exchange ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Lee built Jeet Kune Do against the grain of the traditional schools: not a style to be learned but, as Wikipedia puts it, a principle of “the style of no style.” The water metaphor is that argument compressed into something a television audience could hold in one hand. A cup, a bottle, a teapot — nothing about form, everything about refusing to be committed to one.

What makes the line unusual among famous quotations is that it was engineered for broadcast and then spoken as philosophy by the man who had performed it. Silliphant, an Oscar-winning screenwriter, was also Lee’s student — and by the episode review’s account Lee “worked on the script with Silliphant.” The dialogue credited to Silliphant was close enough to what Lee actually taught that Lee could recite it in an interview as a statement of his own philosophy, which is exactly what he did three months after the episode aired.
detailsBody: The underlying idea was Lee’s long before it was a script. His private writings, collected in Bruce Lee: Artist of Life, describe an epiphany while sailing alone in a junk after a frustrating stretch of training — striking the water and finding it unhurt, and asking whether water was not the very essence of gung fu. The Marginalian on Lee’s water writings ↗

The phrase had a second life half a century on, as a slogan for decentralised, fast-dispersing street protest — which is where a great many people first encountered it, and part of why its 1971 television origin is so often missed.

schema.verdictNote: Attribution traced to a primary source: Lee speaks these words on the 9 December 1971 edition of The Pierre Berton Show. The wording was first heard as dialogue for his character in the Longstreet episode "The Way of the Intercepting Fist", credited to screenwriter Stirling Silliphant; how much of it Lee wrote himself is contested.
